papers.title: CDKL5 deficiency impairs TBK1-mediated autophagy and clearance of neuronal protein aggregates
papers.summary: This paper shows that CDKL5, a kinase whose mutations cause a severe neurodevelopmental disorder, is needed for proper function of TBK1, a protein involved in autophagy. Without CDKL5, neurons fail to efficiently clear damaged proteins and aggregates through autophagy, leading to their buildup. This suggests that defective autophagy is a key mechanism behind the neuronal dysfunction seen in CDKL5 deficiency disorder.
papers.why: This directly supports the project's core interest in mitophagy and autophagy pathways in neurons, offering a molecular mechanism (CDKL5-TBK1 signaling) that could be examined spatially in interneuron populations and correlated with protein aggregate clearance defects.
papers.figure: Figure showing colocalization of protein aggregates with autophagy markers (e.g., LC3/p62) in CDKL5-deficient versus wild-type neurons.

papers.title: spaGFM is a scalable graph foundation model for spatial transcriptomics analyses
papers.summary: spaGFM is a new deep learning model called a 'graph foundation model' designed to analyze spatial transcriptomics data at scale. Spatial transcriptomics maps gene expression while preserving the physical location of cells in tissue, and graph-based models represent cells and their neighbors as networks. spaGFM aims to generalize across many datasets and tasks, potentially serving as a flexible pretrained tool for spatial gene expression analysis.
papers.why: This paper introduces a scalable AI framework for spatial transcriptomics that could be adapted to map interneuron populations and perineuronal net-associated gene expression patterns in brain tissue, directly supporting the spatial transcriptomics and AI/deep learning components of the PhD project.

papers.title: Halo: a pretrained model for whole-cell segmentation from nuclei images in spatial transcriptomics.
papers.summary: Halo is a pretrained deep learning model designed to predict whole-cell boundaries using only nuclei images as input, which is useful for spatial transcriptomics datasets where full-cell membrane staining is unavailable. It likely leverages large-scale training data to generalize across tissue types, enabling accurate cell segmentation without needing dedicated cell-boundary markers. This addresses a major bottleneck in spatial transcriptomics analysis pipelines, where inaccurate cell segmentation can distort gene expression quantification per cell.
papers.why: Accurate whole-cell segmentation from nuclei alone would allow more reliable single-cell resolution analysis of spatial transcriptomics data in brain tissue, including interneurons and cells associated with perineuronal nets, improving downstream mitophagy and autophagy pathway quantification.

papers.title: Ubp3 mediates dynamic deubiquitination of mitochondria upon induction of mitophagy
papers.summary: This study investigates how the deubiquitinating enzyme Ubp3 regulates the removal of ubiquitin marks from mitochondria during the induction of mitophagy. The researchers show that ubiquitination of mitochondrial proteins is a dynamic process, with Ubp3 acting to reverse ubiquitin tagging as mitophagy signaling begins. Their findings suggest that this deubiquitination step is important for properly controlling how damaged or targeted mitochondria are recognized and processed for autophagic clearance.
papers.why: Understanding the molecular machinery of mitophagy regulation via ubiquitin dynamics provides mechanistic insight directly relevant to studying mitochondrial quality control in neurons, which is central to this PhD project.
papers.figure: Figure showing the time-course of ubiquitination/deubiquitination status of mitochondrial proteins before and after mitophagy induction, comparing wild-type versus Ubp3-deficient cells.

papers.title: Dysfunctional mitophagy in Alzheimer's disease: evidence from peripheral Optineurin.
papers.summary: This study examines Optineurin, a key mitophagy receptor protein, in peripheral tissues (likely blood cells) of Alzheimer's disease patients. The findings suggest that mitophagy—the selective clearance of damaged mitochondria—is impaired in AD, as reflected by altered Optineurin levels or function outside the brain. This peripheral marker could serve as a proxy for central nervous system mitochondrial quality control defects in AD.
papers.why: This paper directly supports the PhD focus on mitophagy dysfunction in neurodegeneration, offering a peripheral biomarker angle that could complement spatial transcriptomic/metabolomic studies of mitophagy in brain tissue.

papers.title: Photobiomodulation attenuates corticosterone-induced neuronal injury via activation of the AMPK/ULK1 signaling pathway.
papers.summary: This study looks at how photobiomodulation (light therapy) can protect neurons from damage caused by corticosterone, a stress hormone. The researchers found that this protective effect works through activation of the AMPK/ULK1 signaling pathway, which is a key regulator of autophagy. Essentially, light therapy seems to help neurons survive stress-induced injury by boosting their autophagic machinery.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it directly connects a stress-related neuronal injury model to AMPK/ULK1-mediated autophagy activation, a core mechanistic pathway central to mitophagy and autophagy research in neurons.

papers.title: Species-dependent activities of the PINK1-parkin axis.
papers.summary: This paper likely compares how the PINK1-parkin mitophagy pathway functions differently across species, such as mice versus humans. It probably highlights molecular or biochemical differences that affect how damaged mitochondria are recognized and cleared. Such species-specific findings could explain why some animal models fail to fully replicate human mitochondrial quality control disorders.
papers.why: Understanding species-dependent variation in PINK1-parkin mitophagy activity is crucial for correctly interpreting mouse or other model organism data on neuronal mitophagy before translating findings to human brain tissue.

papers.title: Pretrained gene representations transfer mean expression more broadly than spatial patterns in virtual spatial transcriptomics
papers.summary: This paper investigates whether pretrained gene representations, likely from large-scale genomic or expression foundation models, can help predict spatial gene expression patterns in tissue when only partial spatial transcriptomics data is available. The authors find that these pretrained embeddings are good at transferring information about a gene's average expression level across contexts, but are less effective at capturing the specific spatial patterns of where genes are expressed within tissue. This suggests a gap between general gene expression knowledge and the more complex, context-dependent spatial organization of gene activity.
papers.why: Since the PhD project relies on spatial transcriptomics to map mitophagy and autophagy gene programs in specific neuronal subtypes like interneurons, understanding the limitations of AI-based imputation methods for predicting spatial gene expression patterns is critical for correctly interpreting virtual or extrapolated spatial data.
